items.stem: Which state of matter expands the most for the same temperature rise?
items.answer: Gas
items.markingKey: Gases expand most, then liquids, then solids.

items.stem: Why are gaps left between sections of a railway track?
options: To allow the rails to expand in hot weather without buckling
items.answer: To allow the rails to expand in hot weather without buckling
items.markingKey: Thermal expansion of steel rails.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why solids expand when heated.
items.answer: The particles gain energy and vibrate with larger amplitude, so their average separation increases and the solid gets bigger.
items.markingKey: more vibration [1]; larger separation [1] [2]

items.stem: A steel railway rail 120 m long increases in length by 14.4 mm for every 10 °C rise in temperature. Work out the increase in length for a 20 °C rise.
items.markingKey: 14.4 × 20/10 = 28.8 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A liquid-in-glass thermometer contains alcohol in a thin glass bulb. (a) Explain in terms of particles why the liquid expands when heated. (b) Suggest why alcohol is used instead of mercury for measuring very low temperatures.
items.answer: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average. (b) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C).
items.markingKey: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C) [1]

items.stem: A bimetallic strip bends when heated because …
options: the two metals expand by different amounts
items.answer: the two metals expand by different amounts
items.markingKey: One metal expands more, so the strip curves with that metal on the outside.

items.stem: Explain why a tight metal lid on a glass jar can be loosened by running hot water over it.
items.answer: The metal expands more than the glass for the same temperature rise, so the lid becomes slightly larger and looser.
items.markingKey: metal expands more than glass [1]; lid looser [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why gases expand much more than solids for the same temperature rise.
items.answer: In a gas the forces between particles are negligible, so faster particles easily spread out; in solids strong forces hold the particles close together.
items.markingKey: weak forces in gas [1]; strong forces in solid [1] [2]

items.stem: A concrete motorway section 60 m long increases in length by 7.2 mm for every 10 °C rise. The temperature ranges from 5 °C in winter to 30 °C above that in summer. (a) Calculate the total change in length. (b) Explain why engineers include expansion gaps or joints.
items.answer: (a) 21.6 mm (b) without gaps the expanding structure would push against fixed points, causing large forces that could buckle or crack it.
items.markingKey: (a) 7.2 × 30/10 [1] = 21.6 mm [1] (b) prevents buckling / large forces [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel designs a thermometer for a weather station in Karachi. (a) Explain in terms of particles why the liquid expands when heated. (b) Suggest why alcohol is used instead of mercury for measuring very low temperatures. (c) Name one other device that uses thermal expansion.
items.answer: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average. (b) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C). (c) Bimetallic thermostat (or fire alarm, or fitting a tyre).
items.markingKey: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C) [1] (c) Bimetallic thermostat (or fire alarm, or fitting a tyre) [1]

items.stem: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to …
options: raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
raise the temperature of any mass by 1 °C
items.answer: raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
items.markingKey: c = ΔE/(mΔT).

items.stem: Describe an experiment to measure the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block.
items.answer: Measure the mass of the block; insert an immersion heater and thermometer; record the start temperature; switch on for a measured time with a joulemeter (or P × t); record the final temperature; c = E/(mΔT). Insulate the block.
items.markingKey: mass and temperatures measured [1]; energy from joulemeter or Pt [1]; c = E/(mΔT) [1]; insulation [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why the value of specific heat capacity found in a school experiment is usually higher than the true value.
items.answer: Some of the energy supplied is lost to the surroundings, so the measured temperature rise is smaller than it should be; c = E/(mΔT) comes out too large.
items.markingKey: energy lost to surroundings [1]; ΔT too small → c too large [1] [2]

items.stem: 2010 J raises the temperature of 0.2 kg of a material by 15 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity.
items.markingKey: c = E/(mΔT) = 2010/(0.2 × 15) = 670 J/(kg °C). (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: 200 g of aluminium (c = 900 J/(kg °C)) is heated from 18 °C to 26 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

An immersion heater of power 500 W heats a 2 kg block of ethanol. In 480 s the temperature rises from 18 °C to 68 °C. (a) Calculate the energy supplied. (b) Calculate the specific heat capacity from these results. (c) The accepted value is 2400 J/(kg °C); in a repeat with no insulation the temperature rose by only 42.5 °C. Calculate the value obtained and explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) 240 000 J (b) 2400 J/(kg °C) (c) 2820 J/(kg °C): energy was lost to the surroundings, so ΔT was smaller and c came out too high.

items.stem: In an experiment, a 100 W heater is placed in a 2 kg block of aluminium for 900 s. (a) The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C). Calculate the expected temperature rise. (b) Explain why the measured temperature rise is likely to be less.
items.answer: (a) 50 °C (b) Energy is lost to the surroundings by conduction, convection and radiation.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔT = E/(mc) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 50 °C with unit [1] [2] (b) Energy is lost to the surroundings by conduction [1]; convection and radiation [1] [2]

items.stem: In an experiment, a 100 W heater is placed in a 2 kg block of iron for 600 s. (a) The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J/(kg °C). Calculate the expected temperature rise. (b) Suggest two improvements to the method. (c) State why the temperature should be read a short time after switching off.
items.answer: (a) 66.7 °C (b) Insulate the block; put oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact; use a lid. (c) The temperature keeps rising for a while as thermal energy spreads from the heater through the block.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔT = E/(mc) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 66.7 °C with unit [1] [2] (b) Insulate the block [1]; put oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact, use a lid [1] [2] (c) The temperature keeps rising for a while as thermal energy spreads from the heater through the block [1]

items.stem: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
items.answer: J/(kg °C)
items.markingKey: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

items.stem: Explain why coastal cities often have milder climates than inland cities.
items.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the sea warms and cools slowly, keeping nearby air temperatures more even.
items.markingKey: high shc of water [1]; slow temperature change moderates climate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why water is used in central-heating radiators and car cooling systems.
items.answer: Its high specific heat capacity means each kilogram carries a lot of thermal energy for a given temperature change.
items.markingKey: high shc [1]; carries much energy per kg [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why sweating helps to keep you cool.
items.answer: Sweat evaporates from the skin; the most energetic molecules escape, taking energy from the skin, so the skin cools.
items.markingKey: evaporation [1]; energetic molecules leave, removing energy from skin [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why washing dries faster on a warm, windy day.
items.answer: Warmer water molecules have more energy so more escape; wind removes the vapour so fewer molecules return to the liquid.
items.markingKey: temperature effect [1]; wind removes vapour [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame heats crushed ice and records the temperature every 30 s until it has been boiling for a few minutes. (a) State two differences between this boiling and the evaporation of water from a puddle. (b) Explain why water left in a beaker cools as it evaporates.
items.answer: (a) Boiling at 100 °C throughout the liquid with bubbles; evaporation at any temperature from the surface only. (b) The most energetic particles escape, so the average KE of the remaining particles falls.
items.markingKey: (a) Boiling at 100 °C throughout the liquid with bubbles [1]; evaporation at any temperature from the surface only [1] [2] (b) The most energetic particles escape [1]; so the average KE of the remaining particles falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe an experiment to measure the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. (b) Explain why a burn from steam at 100 °C is more severe than a burn from water at 100 °C.
items.answer: (a) Put crushed ice in a funnel with an immersion heater; collect the meltwater for a measured time with the heater off (control) and on; the extra mass melted by the heater = m; E from joulemeter; l = E/m. (b) Steam releases its large latent heat of vaporisation as it condenses on the skin, in addition to the energy released as the water then cools.
items.markingKey: (a) heater in ice with joulemeter [1]; control funnel to allow for room melting [1]; mass melted measured [1]; l = E/m [1] [4] (b) condensation releases latent heat [1]; extra energy to skin [1] [2]

items.stem: A heating curve for ethanol shows two flat sections. Explain why the second flat section (boiling) is longer than the first (melting) when heated at a constant rate.
items.answer: The specific latent heat of vaporisation is much larger than that of fusion: boiling must separate the particles completely, needing much more energy, which takes longer at the same power.
items.markingKey: flat sections = changes of state [1]; l_v > l_f [1]; more energy at same power takes longer [1] [3]

items.stem: 11 500 J is needed to melt 0.5 kg of lead at constant temperature. Work out the specific latent heat.
items.markingKey: l = E/m = 11 500/0.5 = 23 000 J/kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A 100 W heater is used to melt 20 g of copper at its melting point. Calculate the time needed, assuming all the energy goes to the copper. (specific latent heat = 2.05 × 10⁵ J/kg)

250 g of ice at 0 °C is melted by a 400 W heater (specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg). (a) Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice. (b) Calculate the time the heater takes to supply this energy. (c) The ice actually takes longer to melt. Suggest why.
items.answer: (a) 8.35 × 10⁴ J (b) 209 s (c) Some energy heats the funnel/beaker and surroundings.
items.markingKey: (a) E = lm (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.35 × 10⁴ J [1] [2] (b) t = E/P (method/substitution) [1]; answer 209 s with unit [1] [2] (c) Some energy heats the funnel/beaker and surroundings [1]

items.stem: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because …
options: the liquid contracts as it warms
the glass expands more than the liquid
the liquid expands as its temperature rises
items.answer: the liquid expands as its temperature rises
items.markingKey: The liquid expands more than the glass and rises up the narrow tube.

items.stem: Explain why overhead power cables are hung loosely in summer.
items.answer: In winter they contract; if fitted tight in summer they could snap from the tension when they contract in cold weather.
items.markingKey: contract when cold [1]; avoid breaking [1] [2]

items.stem: A copper pipe 17 m long increases in length by 2.89 mm for every 10 °C rise in temperature. Calculate the increase in length for a 30 °C rise.
items.markingKey: 2.89 × 30/10 = 8.67 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Samuel designs a thermometer for a weather station in Singapore. (a) Explain in terms of particles why the liquid expands when heated. (b) Explain why the bore (tube) of the thermometer is very narrow. (c) Suggest why alcohol is used instead of mercury for measuring very low temperatures. (d) Name one other device that uses thermal expansion.
items.answer: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average. (b) A small expansion of the liquid gives a large rise in the thread, so the thermometer is more sensitive. (c) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C). (d) Bimetallic thermostat (or fire alarm, or fitting a tyre).
items.markingKey: (a) Particles move faster and slightly further apart on average (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) A small expansion of the liquid gives a large rise in the thread [1]; so the thermometer is more sensitive [1] [2] (c) Alcohol has a much lower freezing point (−114 °C) than mercury (−39 °C) [1] (d) Bimetallic thermostat (or fire alarm, or fitting a tyre) [1]

items.stem: Water has a high specific heat capacity. This means it …
options: needs a lot of energy to change its temperature
items.answer: needs a lot of energy to change its temperature
items.markingKey: High c → large energy for small ΔT.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why coastal cities often have milder climates than inland cities. (b) Explain why the value of specific heat capacity found in a school experiment is usually higher than the true value.
items.answer: (a) Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the sea warms and cools slowly, keeping nearby air temperatures more even. (b) Some of the energy supplied is lost to the surroundings, so the measured temperature rise is smaller than it should be; c = E/(mΔT) comes out too large.
items.markingKey: (a) high shc of water [1]; slow temperature change moderates climate [1] [2] (b) energy lost to surroundings [1]; ΔT too small → c too large [1] [2]

items.stem: Equal masses (1 kg) of water (c = 4200 J/(kg °C)) and concrete (c = 880 J/(kg °C)) receive the same amount of energy. Predict which has the larger temperature rise and explain.
items.answer: Concrete: smaller c, so ΔT = E/(mc) is larger.
items.markingKey: correct substance [1]; ΔT ∝ 1/c reasoning [1] [2]

items.stem: 5850 J raises the temperature of 0.5 kg of a material by 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity.
items.markingKey: c = E/(mΔT) = 5850/(0.5 × 30) = 390 J/(kg °C). (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A 0.25 kg mass of aluminium (c = 900 J/(kg °C)) is heated through 40 °C. Calculate the energy needed.
items.markingKey: ΔE = mcΔT = 0.25 × 900 × 40 = 9000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In an experiment, a 100 W heater is placed in a 0.5 kg block of copper for 300 s. (a) The specific heat capacity of copper is 390 J/(kg °C). Calculate the expected temperature rise. (b) Suggest two improvements to the method.
items.answer: (a) 154 °C (b) Insulate the block; put oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact; use a lid.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔT = E/(mc) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 154 °C with unit [1] [2] (b) Insulate the block [1]; put oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact, use a lid [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which change increases the rate of evaporation? (b) Evaporation differs from boiling because evaporation …
items.answer: (a) Blowing air across the surface (b) happens at the surface at any temperature
items.markingKey: (a) Moving air removes vapour; also higher temperature and larger surface area. (b) Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

items.stem: State two factors that affect how quickly sweat on an athlete evaporates and explain, using particles, how each one changes the rate.
items.answer: Wind and humidity: moving air removes escaped particles; a larger surface area lets more particles escape; humid air means more particles return.
items.markingKey: two factors [1]; explanation [1] [2]

items.stem: Liquid paraffin wax is left to cool and its temperature is recorded every minute: 80 °C, 74 °C, 68 °C, 62 °C, 56 °C, 55 °C, 55 °C, 55 °C, 55 °C, 51 °C, 47 °C. (a) State the melting point. (b) Describe the state(s) of the substance during the flat part. (c) Explain why the temperature stays constant there.
items.answer: (a) 55 °C (b) a mixture of liquid and solid: it is solidifying. (c) energy released as particles bond into a solid balances energy lost to the surroundings.
items.markingKey: (a) melting point [1] (b) liquid and solid / freezing [1] (c) energy released on solidifying [1] [3]

items.stem: Liquid stearic acid is left to cool and its temperature is recorded every minute: 84 °C, 78 °C, 74 °C, 69 °C, 69 °C, 69 °C, 69 °C, 66 °C, 62 °C, 59 °C, 56 °C. (a) State the melting point. (b) Describe the state(s) of the substance during the flat part. (c) Explain why the temperature stays constant there.
items.answer: (a) 69 °C (b) a mixture of liquid and solid: it is solidifying. (c) energy released as particles bond into a solid balances energy lost to the surroundings.

items.stem: Ice cubes at 0 °C are heated in a beaker until the water boils. (a) Explain why the temperature stays at 0 °C while the ice melts. (b) Explain why water left in a beaker cools as it evaporates.
items.answer: (a) Energy is used to break bonds between particles, not to raise their KE. (b) The most energetic particles escape, so the average KE of the remaining particles falls.

items.stem: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C and to boil away 0.5 kg of water at 100 °C (l_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg, l_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg), and explain why the second is so much larger.
items.answer: 1.67 × 10⁵ J and 1.13 × 10⁶ J. Boiling separates the particles completely, overcoming almost all the attractive forces, whereas melting only loosens them.
items.markingKey: both energies (E = lm) [1]; boiling must separate particles completely [1]; melting only loosens/rearranges [1] [3]

items.stem: 4.52 × 10⁵ J is needed to boil away 0.2 kg of water at constant temperature. Work out the specific latent heat.
items.markingKey: l = E/m = 4.52 × 10⁵/0.2 = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]
